name: Swimming
summary: Parent-and-baby swimming can start at 3–4 months. Babies get used to water, and from about 4 years children join a swim school without a parent.
why: Builds water confidence early, before fear sets in
Strengthens the whole body and often improves sleep
A calm, close hour together in warm water
steps: Pick a baby or toddler swimming group (beebiujumine / väikelaste ujumine) near you — see the list below.
Book a course on the provider's website: most run 8–10 weekly lessons and start in September and January, but many let you join mid-term if there is space.
Choose a time that doesn't clash with nap time, and feed your child about an hour before.
Buy swim nappies (ujumismähkmed) — reusable ones are cheaper and required in most pools.
At the first lesson arrive 15 minutes early, shower together and keep your child warm between activities.
Between lessons, practise in a warm children's pool at a water park — the parent's calm voice matters more than technique.
bring: Lock coin or bracelet for the locker
price: Usually €12–20 per lesson; a course of 8–10 lessons €100–160. One parent swims free.
howOften: Once a week, 30 minutes in the water.
tips: Under-ones need a warm pool (32–34 °C); ask the provider before booking.
If your child cries the first time, keep it short and come back next week — most settle by the third lesson.
Some swim schools and water parks accept Stebby — look for the Stebby badge.

name: Music
summary: Baby music groups (beebimuusika) welcome children from birth: singing, rhythm, simple instruments and movement with a parent.
why: Easy first group activity — no skills needed
steps: Find a baby or toddler music group in your language — groups are split by age (e.g. 0–1, 1–2, 2–3 years).
Ask for a trial lesson; most groups allow one before you buy a term.
Learn two or three of the group's songs and sing them at home — repetition is what children love.
price: Usually €10–15 per lesson or €80–150 per term.
tips: Library story and song times are a free way to try this first.

name: Toddler gym
summary: Toddler gymnastics (väikelaste võimlemine) is climbing, rolling, balancing and jumping on soft equipment, with a parent until about 3 years.
why: Builds strength, balance and body awareness
Good for confidence and following simple instructions
steps: Choose a parent-and-toddler gym group for your child's age.
Book a trial; dress your child in leggings and a T-shirt, barefoot or in grip socks.
Let your child explore at their own pace — the trainer will guide the circuit.
price: Usually €10–15 per lesson; sports clubs often sell monthly passes.
howOften: Once or twice a week, 45 minutes.
tips: Many gyms and sports clubs accept Stebby.

name: Dance & ballet
summary: Children's dance groups usually start at 2½–3 years and ballet at 3–4 years, without parents in the room.
steps: Check the minimum age — most groups take children who can follow a teacher without a parent (around 3).
Visit an open lesson or trial; studios often hold them in late August and January.
Ask about costumes and end-of-year shows before you sign up.
bring: Ballet shoes or socks (ask the studio)
howOften: Once or twice a week, 30–45 minutes.
tips: Start with one lesson a week; add more only if your child asks for it.

name: Art & messy play
summary: From about one year, sensory and messy-play groups let toddlers paint, squish and explore; art studios for children start at about 3–4 years.
why: Fine motor skills for later writing
Sensory exploration in a place you don't have to clean
steps: For under-threes, look for sensory or messy play sessions (often one-off, no course needed).
From 3–4 years, try a children's art studio (kunstiring) with a term of weekly lessons.
Dress your child in clothes that can get paint on them.
price: Sensory sessions €10–15; art studios €40–60 per month.
howOften: Weekly or whenever you like for drop-in sessions.
tips: Check the Events tab — sensory play mornings appear there.

name: Ice skating
summary: Children can start skating at about 3–4 years; skating schools (uisukool) teach balance and falling safely.
why: A winter activity the whole family can share
Prepares for hockey or figure skating later
steps: Start on an outdoor rink with a skating aid (a penguin or frame) to see if your child enjoys it.
For lessons, join a beginners' group at a skating school — they run from September to spring.
Rent skates at the rink first; buy only once your child wants to continue.
bring: Helmet (required for children at most rinks)
price: Public rinks €3–7 plus skate hire; skating school €50–90 per month.
tips: Go on weekday mornings when rinks are quiet.

name: Skiing
summary: Cross-country or downhill skiing can start at about 3 years with short, playful sessions; ski schools run at Estonian ski centres in winter.
steps: Begin on flat snow at home or in a park with short children's skis.
For lessons, book a children's group at a ski centre (e.g. Nõmme, Kõrvemaa, Otepää) — groups fill quickly in January.
Keep the first sessions to 30–45 minutes and stop while it's still fun.
price: Ski hire €10–20; children's lessons €20–40 per session.
howOften: Whenever there's snow — usually January to March.
tips: Many ski centres rent child-size equipment, so you don't need to buy.

name: Ball games
summary: Kids' football and ball schools take children from about 3–4 years, focusing on play, running and simple ball skills.
steps: Look for a 'mini' group (3–5 years) at a football or ball-games club near you.
Most clubs offer a free trial training — just come in sports clothes.
Ask whether training moves indoors in winter.
bring: Shin guards later, if the club asks
howOften: Once or twice a week, 45 minutes.

name: Nature & forest clubs
summary: Forest and nature clubs (metsaring, loodusring) take children outdoors in all weather to explore, play and learn about plants and animals.
steps: Find a nature club or a nature centre's family programme near you.
Dress for the weather in layers — 'there's no bad weather, only bad clothes'.
Until a club suits you, try free nature trails from the Explore tab.
price: Free to €40 per month; nature centres' family days are often free.
tips: RMK nature trails and many parks are free and stroller-friendly.

name: Language & story time
summary: Libraries run free story and rhyme times for babies and toddlers; language groups (Estonian, English, Russian) help children growing up between languages.
why: Supports a second language — useful for Estonian kindergarten
steps: Check your local library's children's department for baby story or rhyme times.
If your home language isn't Estonian, look for playgroups in Estonian to prepare for kindergarten.
Borrow picture books in both languages and read a little every day.
price: Library events are free; language groups €10–15 per session.
tips: The Events tab lists library events automatically.
